metadata.title: UK Seeks One of World’s Strictest Social Media Bans for Kids

content.text:
(Bloomberg) -- Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced what he described as a "full ban" on children using social media, going beyond limits imposed by Australia last year to create one of the strictest online crackdowns in the democratic world.
"It will make our children safer. It will make our children happier, it will give them more time, more security, more freedom to grow up, more opportunity," Starmer said in a press briefing on Monday morning. In a hint he proceeded with one eye on his own threatened legacy, he added: "That, at the end of the day, is what this government is about."
Starmer is seeking to place his country at the leading edge of a global rush to legislate against the harms of social media, which psychologists have linked to mental health risks. The move sets his government up for a clash with global technology companies, who've chafed against comparable legislation elsewhere.
The prime minister said children under 16 would be prevented from using all major social media platforms, as well as other measures including what he called "world-leading action" to prevent them from speaking to strangers on gaming services and live-streaming platforms without supervision.
But other details of enforcement were sparse, with No. 10 Downing Street saying it would provide further details next month. Results of Australia's own efforts have been mixed, with the regulator reporting in March that about 70% of parents who said their child had social media accounts before the ban still had them.
Starmer's government says its new range of restrictions will be tougher than Australia's limits. Legislation will be passed by the end of the year and the ban will be implemented in spring 2027, the prime minister said. Age verification technology will be used to enforce the restrictions. There will be exemptions for some content, including YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.
"This is not something I do lightly and I will not present it as cost-free," he added. He warned that social media is "designed to be addictive," criticizing "features like infinite scroll" which he said "stops children doing their homework, reading, playing with friends outside and going to bed at a decent time."
Spokespeople for both Snapchat and Google's YouTube told Bloomberg that blanket bans risk pushing children away from curated services toward ones which are less safe. "We share the goal of keeping teens safe online," said a spokesperson for Meta, adding: "Like others, we don't think bans will achieve this goal."
Explainer: How the UK Plans to Keep Children Off Social Media
Asked if he was worried President Donald Trump and US technology companies would be critical of the policy, Starmer said pursuing advances in tech and artificial intelligence and protecting children online were not incompatible. "This is about fighting for what we think is right. I'm a fan of tech and AI," he said.
There will be exemptions for some content, including Google Classroom and YouTube Kids, an app designed for children of eight and below.
Starmer's announcement begins a crucial week for his premiership. He heads to the Group of Seven summit at Évian-les-Bains, France on Monday, where he faces awkward questions following last week's resignation of his defense secretary and uncertainty around the UK's military budget.
Starmer was criticized at the weekend by the father of a teenage girl who took her life in 2017 after being exposed to harmful online content. Ian Russell told the BBC it would be "deplorable" if the prime minister had rushed out the ban as part of a policy blitz before he faces a likely leadership challenge.
A public consultation on how to protect young people closed less than three weeks ago and some of Starmer's cabinet colleagues believe the government's decision to go with a full social media ban for U16s was rushed ahead of Thursday's by-election, according to a person familiar with the situation.
The opposition Liberal Democrats accused the Labour leadership of "rushing through a half-baked policy just to secure a political legacy."
Starmer's primary rival Andy Burnham is expected to win a parliamentary seat at Thursday's special election in Makerfield, northwest England. If Burnham defeats Nigel Farage's populist Reform UK party, he is likely to challenge Starmer, raising the prospect of a summer contest for the keys to No. 10 Downing Street.
Starmer's team is trying to regroup following the resignations of secretary of state John Healey, junior defense minister Al Carns and two ministerial aides last week. Healey said Starmer had failed to secure enough of a spending boost for the military, in light of heightened threats from Russia and other adversaries.
However, Lisa Nandy, the UK's culture secretary, said Sunday that the government had "not finished" trying to find savings from other departments in order to bulk up Britain's defenses.
"Negotiation is happening as we speak," Nandy told the BBC, suggesting that Starmer had decided to look for more money. A larger budget increase would help Starmer meet promises he made to Britain's allies, but — coming after Healey's resignation — risks exposing the premier to accusations of another U-turn.
--With assistance from Joe Mayes, Ellen Milligan and Gian Volpicelli.
(Updates with fresh details on the policy from second paragraph onwards, including reaction from social media companies.)
